name: Example - Nauli Dhara, Dikhet (made-up field answers)

items.comparison: moderate band on the field form scale
items.why: The direct sign of decline, which is what vulnerability means in this project. Daniel et al. 2021 impact group.

items.comparison: moderate band on the field form scale
items.why: A small dry-season flow has little margin left. SOP ch. 5; ICIMOD 2018.

items.comparison: high band on the field form scale
items.why: A big swing means a small or shallow store that empties fast after the rains. SOP ch. 5; Dass et al. 2026.

items.comparison: high band on the field form scale
items.indicator: Months with low or no flow
items.why: Long lean periods leave users short for much of the year. Spring Atlas; SOP.

items.comparison: low band on the field form scale
items.why: Muddy after rain points to shallow, fast flow paths that are easily disturbed.

items.comparison: moderate band on the field form scale
items.why: Kept minor on purpose: a spring that has always been seasonal is not declining; only a change in seasonality is.

items.comparison: moderate band on the field form scale
items.indicator: Households per L/min of lean flow
items.why: Many users on a small flow is the main human pressure. SOP ch. 5; Resource Book.

items.comparison: low band on the field form scale
items.why: Threatens use of the water even if flow holds. SOP ch. 4.

items.comparison: high band on the field form scale
items.why: Cuts infiltration in the likely recharge area. Daniel 2021; SOP.

items.comparison: low band on the field form scale
items.why: Protected, managed springs are looked after when problems start. Resource Book; SOP ch. 6.

items.comparison: high band on the field form scale
items.why: Trenches, pits and plantation uphill raise recharge (Mathamali: 5.7 to 19.5 L/min). Daniel 2021.

items.comparison: 211 mm falls in November-April on average; 37% of the input springs get more.
items.why: Winter and pre-monsoon rain feeds the spring in the months it is lowest. Daniel 2021 rainfall stressor.

items.comparison: Yearly rain is 1.36 times the evaporation demand; 66% of the input springs are wetter.
items.why: Less water left over for recharge after evaporation.

items.comparison: Yearly rain varies by 13% from year to year; 56% of the input springs vary less.
items.why: Dry years hit harder where rain swings a lot. Only 8 years of data, so a weak signal.

items.comparison: 2% of the land within 500 m is built-up, cropland or bare; 38% of the input springs have less.
items.indicator: Built-up, cropland and bare land within 500 m
items.why: Less forest and more sealed or tilled land means less infiltration near the spring. Stand-in until Module B maps the real recharge zone.

items.comparison: Mean slope within 500 m is 19 degrees; 16% of the input springs sit on gentler ground.
items.why: Steep slopes shed rain as runoff before it can soak in.

items.comparison: The land rises 274 m above the spring within 1 km; 63% of the input springs have more land above them.
items.indicator: Land rising above the spring within 1 km
items.why: A spring close to a ridge top has little land above it to collect recharge.
